# Creating a Java Container Image with an Agent Skill

This example packages a small Java application and includes a reusable Codex
skill that can containerise Java source projects. The skill brings together the
workshop concerns that apply to a real container image: build inputs, Oracle
Java base images, layer reuse, an unprivileged runtime user, diagnostics, slim
runtimes, startup optimisation, and architecture.

A Dockerfile that builds is not sufficient evidence that its image is suitable
for an application. In this example, you will inspect the project facts the
skill uses, establish a working packaged JAR, and review the Dockerfile it
generates from an explicitly approved base image.

It deliberately does not try every technique automatically. `jlink`, CDS,
Project Leyden AOT caches, diagnostics, and multi-architecture builds each have
constraints that source inspection cannot settle reliably. The skill therefore
uses a straightforward Oracle Java JDK image as its baseline and asks for
clarification before choosing a specialised strategy.

This is a focused example. It does not cover every aspect of running Java in
containers; see the
[all-in-one Spring Boot example](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md) for a more
holistic example.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect the project facts that constrain a Java container image;
- build and verify the packaged application artefact before containerising it;
- review a Dockerfile generated from a confirmed image strategy; and
- explain why image size, startup optimisation, diagnostics, and target
  architectures require explicit deployment constraints.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with a running daemon

- `codex`, and `crane`, used to invoke the skill and resolve the
  immutable base-image reference.

The optional local application check also uses `curl`, `jq`, and `tree` to wait
for the endpoint, format its response, and inspect the build output. Install
them if you plan to run that part of the walkthrough.

### Oracle Container Registry access

Before pulling an Oracle Java base image, sign in to Oracle Container Registry
and accept the terms for the
[Oracle Java JDK repository](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk).

1. Accept the Oracle Container Registry terms.

2. Authenticate your container engine with your own Oracle Container Registry
   username and authentication token.

   Pass the token through standard input so it is neither recorded in shell
   history nor copied into the project or image layers. If you use Podman, use
   its equivalent `login --password-stdin` command.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

3. Verify that the container engine can pull and run the Oracle Java JDK image.

   ```shell
   docker run --rm 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' java --version
   ```

   Docker pulls the image if necessary, then prints the Java runtime version.

   ```
   java 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18 LTS
   Java(TM) SE Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5)
   Java HotSpot(TM) 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS-5, mixed mode, sharing)
   ```

## The artefacts to inspect

The input is this Maven project, not merely the Java source file. Its `pom.xml`
establishes Java 25 and Spring Boot packaging, while the application source
establishes the entry point. Together, they allow the skill to discover how to
build and start the application. A project with missing build metadata or an
ambiguous entry point must cause the skill to ask a question, not invent a
Dockerfile that happens to compile.

```xml
...
    <parent>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
        <version>4.1.1</version>
        <relativePath/>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>agent-container-image-java</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0</version>
    <name>Agent-assisted Spring Boot Container Image</name>
    <description>
        A Spring Boot web application used to demonstrate an agent skill that
        creates a container image from application source code.
    </description>

    <properties>
        <java.version>25</java.version>
...
```

The application’s `Main.java` starts the Spring Boot service. The packaged JAR
combines this application code with the Spring Boot launcher and dependencies;
it is the controlled input that the generated Dockerfile must run.

```java
package demo;

import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.boot.CommandLineRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;

import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;
import java.util.List;

@SpringBootApplication
public class Main {

    private static final Logger LOGGER = LoggerFactory.getLogger(Main.class);

    static void main(final String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(Main.class, args);
    }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner javaVersionRunner() { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner processRunner() { /* Closed for brevity */ }

    @Bean
    CommandLineRunner configurationRunner() { /* Closed for brevity */ }
}
```

## Build the application

Build the application once before asking the skill to produce a Dockerfile. The
resulting executable JAR is used for the local runtime check and is the known
artefact that the baseline container strategy copies into the image.

1. Build the application

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── agent-container-image-java-1.0.0.jar
   └── agent-container-image-java-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. (*Optional*) Run the packaged application

   This starts the JAR outside a container. A successful endpoint response
   establishes that the application artefact works before its runtime layout is
   changed by container packaging.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/agent-container-image-java-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote. A JSON response confirms that the packaged service is
   running and can serve its endpoint.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Albert Einstein",
     "id": 15,
     "quote": "Weakness of attitude becomes weakness of character."
   }
   ```

   Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run the remaining commands from this example directory. They inspect the skill,
supply the confirmed project facts, and leave a Dockerfile for review; they do
not build or push an image.

The skill is stored with the example so participants can inspect its complete
instruction set. It should create `containers/Dockerfile` only after confirming
the discovered project facts and image strategy. The following excerpt shows the
facts it discovers, when it must ask for clarification, and how it selects a
packaging strategy.

1. Discover the skill

   Codex discovers repository-local skills from `.agents/skills` in the current
   directory and its parent directories up to the repository root. This example
   already stores the skill at `.agents/skills/java-container-image`. Start
   Codex from this example directory, or from one of its subdirectories, so the
   skill is available.

   (*Optional*) List the skill files

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name '.agents/skills/java-container-image'
   ```

   The skill files

   ```
   .agents/skills/java-container-image
   ├── agents
   │   └── openai.yaml
   └── SKILL.md

   2 directories, 2 files
   ```

   If Codex was already open when the skill was added or changed, refresh the
   skills before continuing.

2. Use the skill

   Prompt the model to use the `java-container-image` skill to create the
   container image.

   > Use the $java-container-image skill to create a Dockerfile for this project. Use the local image tag `demo:agent-container-image`. Do not build or push the image yet.

   To run this in unattended mode, provide all required information upfront. Log
   in to the container registry first if you have not already do so.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

   Prompt the model.

   > Use the $java-container-image skill to create a Dockerfile for this project. Use the local image tag `demo:agent-container-image`. Do not build or push the image.

   Alternatively, run this autonomously without interacting with the TUI.

   ```shell
   BASE_IMAGE="container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1@$(crane digest 'container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1')"

   codex exec \
     --ephemeral \
     --sandbox workspace-write \
     --model gpt-6.1-sol \
     --config 'model_reasoning_effort="medium"' \
     --skip-git-repo-check \
     --output-last-message './target/codex-create-java-container-image.md' \
     - <<EOF > './target/codex-create-java-container-image.log' 2>&1
   Use the \$java-container-image skill to create a Dockerfile for this project.
   Use the local image tag \`demo:agent-container-image\`.
   Do not build or push the image.

   For this workshop run only, I approve this resolved Oracle Java base image:
   \`${BASE_IMAGE}\`
   Use it unchanged in the Dockerfile. Do not ask for further approval.
   EOF
   ```

   Read the model result. It should identify the confirmed base-image reference
   and report the generated Dockerfile without claiming that the image was
   built.

   ```markdown
   Created [containers/Dockerfile](/home/opc/workspace/workshop-java-in-containers/examples/agent-container-image-java/containers/Dockerfile) and restrictive [.dockerignore](/home/opc/workspace/workshop-java-in-containers/examples/agent-container-image-java/.dockerignore).

   Uses your approved base unchanged, copies the verified Java 25 executable JAR, runs as `10001:0`, and exposes `8080`. Includes the build command for tag `demo:agent-container-image`.

   Static checks passed. No image was built or pushed; container execution remains unverified.
   ```

   Inspect the generated Dockerfile. Confirm that it uses the approved immutable
   base-image reference and that its entry point, artefact path, and runtime
   user match the project facts established earlier.

   ```Dockerfile
   # Run from the project root when an image build is requested:
   # docker build -f containers/Dockerfile -t demo:agent-container-image .
   FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1@sha256:947650420cbf1a8d0ade992ed0cdc2edab4f8d4da1b80f501a56d3392e09e921

   ARG JAR_FILE=target/agent-container-image-java-1.0.0.jar
   WORKDIR /app
   COPY --chown=10001:0 ${JAR_FILE} /app/application.jar

   USER 10001:0
   EXPOSE 8080
   ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/application.jar"]
   ```

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- The Maven project, its Java version, the executable JAR, and runtime
  requirements are evidence for the image design; source files alone are not.
- A working JAR is a controlled baseline, but it does not by itself validate a
  container image or its deployment configuration.
- The baseline copies a verified JAR into an Oracle Java JDK image; a slimmer
  runtime, startup optimisation, diagnostics, or multiple architectures need
  explicit goals and validation.
- The generated Dockerfile is a proposal to review. A successful image build is
  not approval for production use.
